levels.29.title: A closed circuit
levels.29.intro: Until now everything was a tree. But nature also allows stories that loop back on themselves: loops.
levels.29.steps.loop.prompt: This diagram has a loop. Select all the lines that form the closed circuit.
levels.29.steps.loop.wrongDefault: That line isn't part of the circuit. Look for a path that leaves a vertex and comes back to it.
levels.29.steps.loop.hints.0: Start from the top-left vertex and look for a path back to it without repeating lines.
levels.29.steps.loop.hints.1: The loop is made of the curved photon at the top and the two electron segments below it.
levels.29.steps.loop.solved: That's the loop: a photon emitted and reabsorbed by the same electron.
levels.29.steps.momentum.prompt: In a tree, momentum conservation fixes the momentum of each internal line. What happens with the lines of a loop?
levels.29.steps.momentum.options.fixed.f: In a closed circuit momentum can “go round” without the external particles noticing.
levels.29.steps.momentum.options.all.tex: It can have any value and you have to add them all up
levels.29.steps.momentum.options.all.fee: Each loop adds an integral over a free momentum.
levels.29.steps.momentum.options.zero.fe: Nothing forces it to be zero: any value is compatible with conservation.
levels.29.steps.momentum.hints.0: Imagine an amount of momentum entering the loop and going all the way round.
levels.29.steps.momentum.hints.1: The external particles can't know how much momentum circulates inside.
levels.29.steps.order.prompt: This diagram has 4 vertices. How much smaller is its amplitude than that of the Møller tree?
levels.29.steps.order.options.e2.text: A factor e², that is, ∝ α
levels.29.steps.order.options.e2.feedbac: Two more vertices: e⁴ versus e². That's why loops are small corrections.
levels.29.steps.order.hints.0: Amplitude ∝ eⁿ, with n the number of vertices.
levels.29.success: You can now recognise a loop and you know why it's a small correction.
levels.29.explanation.intuitive: In a loop, the virtual particle can carry any amount of momentum. Nature tries them all.
levels.29.explanation.scientific: Each independent loop leaves a momentum that isn't fixed by conservation at the vertices; you have to integrate over it. These integrals can diverge, and renormalization is the technique that tames them. Each loop adds two vertices: a factor α in the relative amplitude.
levels.29.explanation.math: 𝓜₁ ∝ e⁴ ∫ d⁴ℓ/(2π)⁴ [propagators with ℓ]. Loops: L = I − V + 1, with I internal lines and V vertices.
levels.30.title: The vacuum boils
levels.30.intro: The photon exchanged by two electrons can turn, for an instant, into an electron–positron pair and become a photon again.
levels.30.steps.build.prompt: Complete the loop between the two central vertices: the virtual photon turns into an e⁻e⁺ pair that annihilates again.
levels.30.steps.build.hints.0: Each central vertex already has its photon. It's missing the two fermion lines.
levels.30.steps.build.hints.1: Draw two fermion lines between the two central vertices, with arrows in opposite directions. The second one curves by itself.
levels.30.steps.effect.prompt: These virtual pairs surround each electron like a cloud that screens its charge. What happens when you get very close to the electron (at high energies)?
levels.30.steps.effect.options.more.text: You get through the cloud and the effective charge increases
levels.30.steps.effect.options.more.feed: α grows with energy: from ≈ 1/137 to ≈ 1/128 at the energy of the Z boson.
levels.30.steps.effect.options.less.feed: The opposite happens: the cloud screens, so inside it you see more charge.
levels.30.steps.effect.options.same.text: The charge is always the same
levels.30.steps.effect.options.same.feed: The “bare” charge doesn't change, but the one we measure depends on the distance.
levels.30.steps.effect.hints.0: Think of the cloud of pairs as a dielectric surrounding the charge.
levels.30.steps.effect.hints.1: Inside the cloud there's less screening.
levels.30.success: You've drawn vacuum polarization: the quantum vacuum isn't empty.
levels.30.explanation.intuitive: Empty space is full of particle–antiparticle pairs that appear and disappear. They surround each charge and screen it.
levels.30.explanation.scientific: Vacuum polarization makes the coupling constant depend on energy: α(0) ≈ 1/137, but α(m_Z) ≈ 1/128. It was the first “constant” seen to change, and the contribution can be measured in the Lamb shift of hydrogen.
levels.30.explanation.math: Π(q²) ≈ (α/3π) ln(−q²/m²) for |q²| ≫ m²; α_eff(q²) = α / (1 − Π(q²)).
levels.31.title: Schwinger's number
levels.31.intro: An electron crosses a magnetic field. In 1948, Julian Schwinger calculated how a loop changes its internal magnet. The result is engraved on his tombstone.
levels.31.steps.build.prompt: Build the vertex correction: the electron emits a virtual photon, interacts with the field and reabsorbs the photon.
levels.31.steps.build.hints.0: The electron line passes through all three vertices: left, middle and right.
levels.31.steps.build.hints.1: Electron → left → middle → right → exit, and a photon joins the left vertex to the right one.
levels.31.steps.g2.prompt: Without the loop, the electron's “g-factor” is exactly 2. The loop corrects it: a = (g − 2)/2. What is that correction?
levels.31.steps.g2.options.half.feedback: It's a one-loop correction: it must be of order α.
levels.31.steps.g2.options.schwinger.fee: Schwinger's result. Today it's known up to five loops and agrees with experiment to more than 10 digits.
levels.31.steps.g2.options.zero.feedback: If it were zero, the loop would have no effect. It does, and it's measured.
levels.31.steps.g2.hints.0: A loop contributes a factor α compared with the tree.
levels.31.steps.g2.hints.1: α ≈ 1/137, and it appears divided by 2π.
levels.31.success: You've drawn one of the most famous diagrams in physics.
levels.31.explanation.intuitive: The electron isn't alone: it carries a cloud of virtual photons that slightly changes how it responds to a magnet.
levels.31.explanation.scientific: The electron's anomalous magnetic moment, a = α/2π at one loop, is the most precise prediction in physics: theory and experiment agree to more than 10 significant figures. With this arrangement of vertices another one-loop correction is also valid: the self-energy of an external line.
levels.31.explanation.math: Γ^μ = γ^μ F₁(q²) + (iσ^{μν}q_ν / 2m) F₂(q²), with a = F₂(0) = α/2π + 𝒪(α²).
levels.32.title: Light on light
levels.32.intro: Two beams of light cross without touching... almost always. Can a photon bounce off another?
levels.32.steps.tree.prompt: Is there any tree-level diagram (without loops) for γγ → γγ?
levels.32.steps.tree.options.yes.text: Yes, joining the four photons at two vertices
levels.32.steps.tree.options.yes.feedbac: Each QED vertex needs two fermion lines. Here no fermion comes in or goes out.
levels.32.steps.tree.options.no.text: No: with no external fermions, the fermion lines have to close into a loop
levels.32.steps.tree.hints.0: Count how many fermion lines each vertex needs.
levels.32.steps.tree.hints.1: A fermion line can only end at an edge or carry on. If there are no fermions at the edges...
levels.32.steps.box.prompt: Build the box diagram: join the four vertices with fermion lines.
levels.32.steps.box.hints.0: Each vertex already has its photon. It's missing an arrow coming in and one going out.
levels.32.steps.box.hints.1: Go round the square in a single direction: top-left → top-right → bottom-right → bottom-left → back to the start.
levels.32.success: Light can scatter light, but only through a loop of virtual matter.
levels.32.explanation.intuitive: Photons don't interact directly: they need the vacuum to lend them, for an instant, an electron and a positron.
levels.32.explanation.scientific: Light-by-light scattering doesn't exist in classical physics and in QED it first appears at one loop. There are 6 box diagrams. ATLAS observed it in 2017 in collisions of lead ions, whose huge electric fields act as photon beams.
levels.32.explanation.math: 𝓜(γγ → γγ) ∝ e⁴, σ ∝ α⁴. At low energy, the effect is described by the Euler–Heisenberg Lagrangian.
levels.33.title: Furry's theorem
levels.33.intro: Some diagrams follow every rule and, even so, their total contribution is exactly zero.
levels.33.steps.impostor.prompt: Which of these loops does NOT contribute to any process?
levels.33.steps.impostor.options.box.fee: The four-photon box exists: it's light-by-light scattering.
This bubble is vacuum polarization: it has measurable effects.
levels.33.steps.impostor.options.triangl: An electron loop with an odd number of photons cancels out.
levels.33.steps.impostor.hints.0: Count how many photons attach to each electron loop.
levels.33.steps.impostor.hints.1: Look for the loop with an odd number of photons.
levels.33.steps.cancel.prompt: The triangle can be traversed in both directions. Both diagrams are valid. What happens when you add them?
levels.33.steps.cancel.diagrams.0.label: Clockwise
levels.33.steps.cancel.diagrams.1.label: Anticlockwise
levels.33.steps.cancel.options.double.te: They add up: the effect doubles
levels.33.steps.cancel.options.double.fe: Reversing the loop is the same as swapping electron for positron, and each photon changes sign under that operation.
levels.33.steps.cancel.options.cancel.fe: With 3 photons, reversing the loop gives a sign (−1)³ = −1.
levels.33.steps.cancel.options.partial.f: The cancellation is exact, for any photon momenta.
levels.33.steps.cancel.hints.0: Reversing the arrows is the same as swapping electrons for positrons.
levels.33.steps.cancel.hints.1: Each photon contributes a sign −1 under that operation.
levels.33.success: You've spotted a valid diagram that contributes nothing: a symmetry cancels it.
levels.33.explanation.intuitive: Two identical stories, but traversed in opposite directions, balance each other perfectly.
levels.33.explanation.scientific: Furry's theorem (1937) says that a closed electron loop with an odd number of photons doesn't contribute. It's a consequence of charge-conjugation symmetry: the photon is odd under C. The game's validator applies it: if you build a loop like that, it will warn you.
levels.33.explanation.math: C A_μ C⁻¹ = −A_μ ⇒ ⟨0|T{A_μ₁ ⋯ A_μₙ}|0⟩ = 0 for odd n. The two orientations add to 𝓜 + (−1)ⁿ𝓜.
levels.34.title: Grand finale: Møller at one loop
levels.34.intro: A PhD student's exam: go beyond the tree in electron–electron scattering.
levels.34.steps.box.prompt: Build a one-loop correction to e⁻e⁻ → e⁻e⁻ using all four vertices. Try the box diagram: the electrons exchange two photons.
levels.34.steps.box.hints.0: Each electron passes through two vertices: the top one through the top two, the bottom one through the bottom two.
levels.34.steps.box.hints.1: 1 → top-left → top-right → 3; 2 → bottom-left → bottom-right → 4; and two vertical photons between the two lines.
levels.34.steps.interference.prompt: The probability is |𝓜_tree + 𝓜_loop|². The loop's first effect is the cross term 2·Re(𝓜_tree* · 𝓜_loop). At what order does it contribute?
The tree alone already gives α². The cross term has more vertices.
α³: an order-α correction to the tree result
e² · e⁴ = e⁶ ∝ α³. That's why the tree is enough for ~1% precision.
levels.34.steps.interference.hints.1: Multiply: e² · e⁴, and remember that α ∝ e².
levels.34.success: Campaign complete. You've gone from the quantum alphabet to one-loop corrections.
levels.34.explanation.intuitive: Each level of detail adds more complicated stories, and each one weighs about a hundred times less than the one before. That's how QED can make such astonishingly precise predictions.
levels.34.explanation.scientific: At one loop, Møller scattering gets vertex, vacuum polarization, self-energy and box (direct and crossed) corrections. They're all ∝ α relative to the tree, and some have infrared divergences that only cancel when you add the braking radiation from chapter 6.
levels.34.explanation.math: σ = σ₀ [1 + (α/π) C + 𝒪(α²)], with σ₀ ∝ α². The infrared divergences cancel between ee → ee (one loop) and ee → eeγ (Bloch–Nordsieck theorem).
